A minimal quantum-particle-detector model demonstrating fundamental trade-offs between entropy production and measurement accuracy is presented, providing new insights into the thermodynamic cost of information acquisition.


[PRX Quantum 7, 033001] Published Wed Jul 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a minimal quantum-particle-detector model that reveals fundamental trade-offs between entropy production and measurement accuracy, providing new insights into the thermodynamic cost of information acquisition.
motivation: Understanding the thermodynamic cost of information acquisition is crucial for designing efficient quantum detectors and information processing devices. The authors aim to bridge quantum measurement and thermodynamics by analyzing a minimal model.
method: They introduce a minimal quantum-particle-detector model and analyze its nonequilibrium thermodynamics, likely using concepts from quantum thermodynamics and information theory to quantify entropy production and measurement accuracy.
result: The model demonstrates fundamental trade-offs between entropy production and measurement accuracy, indicating that more accurate measurements require higher thermodynamic cost.
conclusion: The findings provide new insights into the thermodynamic cost of information acquisition, which is relevant for quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Continuous-variable Quantum Communication
authors: Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, And Valerio Pruneri
abstract:
Author(s): Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, and Valerio Pruneri

The quantum nature of radiation is not solely corpuscular. In the “continuous-variable” setting, the wavelike quantum properties can be observed. Quantum technologies put this continuous-variable nature of light to use, with applications in various forms of quantum information processing. This review concentrates on the developments of these wave-based techniques in quantum communication. Compared with photon-based (corpuscular) variants, the continuous-variable approach is equally well developed and has certain conceptual and practical advantages.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015003] Published Mon Mar 23, 2026.
tldr: A comprehensive review of continuous-variable quantum communication, covering protocols, security, and implementations.
motivation: To provide an up-to-date overview of the continuous-variable approach to quantum communication, highlighting its advantages and recent developments.
method: The paper reviews the theoretical foundations, protocols (e.g., QKD, entanglement-based), security proofs, and experimental implementations of continuous-variable quantum communication.
result: Summarizes the state of the art, including security proofs and experimental demonstrations, and discusses future directions.
conclusion: Continuous-variable quantum communication is a mature and promising field with practical advantages, and the review consolidates its progress and potential.

title: Quantum Cryptography Beyond Key Distribution: Theory And Experiment
authors: Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, And Philip Walther
abstract:
Author(s): Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, and Philip Walther

Cryptography not only involves the sending of secret messages but also encompasses many protocols and procedures that provide privacy and security in the networked world. Likewise, quantum resources have the potential to enhance cryptography in ways that go beyond the well-known example of quantum key distribution. This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. It explains the security that they offer, including the sometimes significant limitations on their theoretical capabilities. Implementations using current photonic techniques are discussed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045006] Published Fri Dec 19, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory, security, and photonic implementations.
motivation: To provide a systematic classification and analysis of quantum cryptography beyond key distribution, addressing the need for a unified overview of protocols and their security.
method: The authors review and classify various quantum cryptographic primitives, discussing their theoretical security guarantees and limitations, and survey current photonic implementations.
result: The review presents a taxonomy of quantum crypto primitives, highlights security challenges, and summarizes experimental progress in photonic platforms.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers a rich landscape of protocols beyond QKD, with practical implementations emerging, though many face significant theoretical and experimental hurdles.

title: Catalytic $z$-rotations In Constant $T$-depth
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2191 (2026).

We show that the [MATH]-depth of any single-qubit [MATH]-rotation can be reduced to [MATH] if a certain catalyst state is available. To achieve an [MATH]-approximation, it suffices to have a catalyst state of size polynomial in [MATH]. This implies that [MATH] admits a finite universal gate set consisting of Clifford+[MATH]. In particular, there are catalytic constant [MATH]-depth circuits that approximate multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform arbitrarily well. We also show that the catalyst state can be prepared in time polynomial in [MATH].

.
tldr: This paper shows that any single-qubit z-rotation can be approximated to arbitrary precision with constant T-depth using a catalyst state of polynomial size, implying a finite universal gate set for quantum computation.
motivation: Reducing T-depth is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation, as T gates are expensive. The paper aims to achieve constant T-depth for arbitrary rotations, which was previously thought to require non-constant depth.
method: The authors construct a catalyst state that enables the implementation of any z-rotation with constant T-depth, using a technique that leverages the catalyst to absorb the approximation error. They also provide a polynomial-time preparation of the catalyst state.
result: They prove that any single-qubit z-rotation can be approximated with constant T-depth, and that the catalyst state size scales polynomially with the approximation precision. This leads to constant T-depth circuits for multi-qubit gates like Toffoli, adder, and QFT.
conclusion: The result establishes that a finite universal gate set (Clifford+T) suffices for constant T-depth quantum computation, which has significant implications for fault-tolerant quantum computing resource optimization.

title: Unconditional Quantum Advantage For Sampling With Shallow Circuits
authors: Adam Bene Watts And Natalie Parham
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2188 (2026).

Recent work by Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig showed that there exists a search problem that a constant-depth quantum circuit can solve, but that any constant-depth classical circuit with bounded fan-in cannot. They also pose the question: Can we achieve a similar proof of separation for an input-independent sampling task? In this paper, we show that the answer to this question is yes when the number of random input bits given to the classical circuit is bounded. We introduce a distribution [MATH] over [MATH] and construct a constant-depth uniform quantum circuit family [MATH] such that [MATH] samples from a distribution close to [MATH] in total variation distance. For any [MATH] we also prove, unconditionally, that any classical circuit with bounded fan-in gates that takes as input [MATH] i.i.d. Bernouli random variables with entropy [MATH] and produces output close to [MATH] in total variation distance has depth [MATH]. This gives an unconditional proof that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from distributions that can't be reproduced by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits, even up to additive error. We also show a similar separation between constant-depth quantum circuits with advice and classical circuits with bounded fan-in and fan-out, but access to an unbounded number of i.i.d random inputs. The distribution [MATH] and classical circuit lower bounds are inspired by work of Viola, in which he shows a different (but related) distribution cannot be sampled from approximately by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits.

.
tldr: This paper proves an unconditional separation between constant-depth quantum and classical circuits for a sampling task, showing that quantum circuits can sample from a distribution that classical circuits of bounded depth cannot approximate.
motivation: The authors aim to extend the known separation for search problems to sampling tasks, which is a fundamental question in quantum computational advantage. They address a question posed by Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig.
method: They introduce a specific distribution and construct a constant-depth quantum circuit that samples from it. They then prove, using techniques inspired by Viola, that any classical circuit with bounded fan-in and limited random input bits requires depth that grows with the number of bits to approximate the distribution.
result: They show that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from a distribution that cannot be reproduced by constant-depth classical circuits with bounded fan-in, even with additive error, under the condition that the classical circuit has limited random input bits. They also show a similar separation for circuits with advice.
conclusion: This provides an unconditional quantum advantage for sampling with shallow circuits, strengthening the case for quantum computational superiority in a practical setting.

title: Quantifiers And Witnesses For The Nonclassicality Of Measurements And Of States
authors: Yujie Zhang, Yìlè Yīng, And David Schmid
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2180 (2026).

In recent work [Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050], we proposed a unified notion of nonclassicality that applies to arbitrary processes in quantum theory, including individual quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof. This notion is derived from the principle of generalized noncontextuality, but in a novel manner that applies to individual processes rather than full experiments or theories. In the present work, we develop semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of states, sources, measurements, and sets thereof. These theory-dependent methods complement theory-independent approaches based on noncontextuality inequalities. We demonstrate the framework through a variety of explicit examples.

.
tldr: This paper develops semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for nonclassicality of quantum states and measurements, based on generalized noncontextuality.
motivation: To provide practical tools for detecting nonclassicality in individual quantum processes, complementing theory-independent noncontextuality inequalities.
method: The authors formulate nonclassicality as a semidefinite programming problem, deriving certificates and witnesses for states, sources, and measurements, and demonstrate them with examples.
result: They present explicit SDP-based methods that can certify nonclassicality in various scenarios, offering a unified framework for states and measurements.
conclusion: The work advances the operational characterization of nonclassicality, providing useful tools for quantum information tasks.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

.
tldr: This paper connects Barnes Wall lattices to stabilizer ranks and introduces a new magic monotone, providing improved lower bounds and a fidelity amplification algorithm.
motivation: The authors aim to deepen the understanding of stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, which are central to quantum resource theories and quantum computing.
method: They leverage the connection between Barnes Wall lattices and stabilizer states, define a new magic monotone (Barnes Wall norm), and provide proofs for lower bounds and algorithmic trade-offs.
result: They establish the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, show tight upper bounds for the new monotone, and provide a fidelity amplification algorithm.
conclusion: The work advances the theory of stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, offering new tools for quantum resource estimation and potential applications in quantum computing.

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: This paper provides a complete theory of the Clifford commutant, offering explicit bases and a graphical calculus, with applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: The Clifford group is central to quantum information, but the structure of its commutant was only partially understood for small tensor powers. A complete characterization is needed for deeper insights into pseudorandomness, learning, and entanglement distillation.
method: The authors develop an explicit orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant for arbitrary tensor power and qubit number, introduce an alternative basis of isotropic sums of Pauli operators, and provide a graphical calculus for manipulating these elements.
result: They compute the dimension of the commutant, show the basis is generated by permutations and at most three other operators, and apply the theory to characterize measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing.
conclusion: The complete theory of the Clifford commutant opens up new applications in quantum information, including operational interpretations of stabilizer entropies and generalizations to qudit systems.

title: Equivalence Of Quantum Resources Under Ergodic Dynamics
authors: Sreemayee Aditya, Xhek Turkeshi, Piotr Sierant
abstract: ArXiv:2608.15197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum resource theories characterize distinct forms of nonclassicality in many-body quantum states, raising the question of whether these resources evolve independently under generic ergodic dynamics. Considering diagnostics quadratic in the state, we show that the dynamics of different resource measures become mutually interdependent and are governed by a few common degrees of freedom. For Haar-random circuits, the purity together with a single resource witness suffices to reconstruct the remaining resource measures, as we demonstrate for coherence, various asymmetries, and number entropies. The same relations hold, to a good approximation, under chaotic Floquet and continuous-time Hamiltonian dynamics, establishing that this dynamical resource equivalence extends beyond random circuits. We further derive an exact coherence--imaginarity relation, remarkably accurate also beyond Haar-random circuits. Our results reveal an emergent simplification of many-body dynamics, in which sufficiently strong scrambling reduces seemingly distinct quantum resources to a few common dynamical degrees of freedom.
tldr: This paper shows that under ergodic dynamics, different quantum resource measures become interdependent and can be reconstructed from a few common degrees of freedom, revealing an emergent simplification of many-body dynamics.
motivation: Understanding how distinct quantum resources evolve under generic dynamics is fundamental to quantum information and many-body physics, with implications for resource theories and quantum technologies.
method: The authors analyze diagnostics quadratic in the state for Haar-random circuits, chaotic Floquet, and continuous-time Hamiltonian dynamics, deriving relations between resource measures such as coherence, asymmetry, and number entropies.
result: They demonstrate that purity plus a single resource witness suffices to reconstruct other resource measures, and derive an exact coherence-imaginarity relation that holds beyond Haar-random circuits.
conclusion: The results establish a dynamical resource equivalence under strong scrambling, simplifying the description of quantum resources in ergodic systems.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the dynamical interrelations among different quantum resource measures in many-body systems undergoing ergodic dynamics. The authors focus on diagnostics that are quadratic in the quantum state, such as purity and linear entropies, and demonstrate that under Haar-random unitary circuits, the dynamics of various resource measures (coherence, asymmetry, number entropy) become mutually interdependent and can be reconstructed from a few common degrees of freedom—specifically, the purity and a single resource witness. They derive exact relations for Haar-random circuits and show that these relations hold approximately for chaotic Floquet and continuous-time Hamiltonian dynamics, indicating an emergent simplification in strongly scrambling dynamics. Additionally, they derive an exact coherence–imaginarity relation that remains accurate beyond Haar-random circuits. The results suggest that distinct quantum resources do not evolve independently but are governed by a few common dynamical variables, providing a new perspective on the universality of many-body quantum dynamics.
key_contributions: Demonstration that for Haar-random circuits, the dynamics of multiple quantum resource measures (coherence, asymmetry, number entropy) are determined by purity and a single resource witness, leading to exact reconstruction formulas.
Establishment of approximate validity of these resource equivalence relations under chaotic Floquet and continuous-time Hamiltonian dynamics, extending the results beyond random circuits.
Derivation of an exact coherence–imaginarity relation that holds with high accuracy even outside the Haar-random setting.
Introduction of the concept of 'dynamical resource equivalence,' showing that strong scrambling reduces seemingly distinct quantum resources to a few common dynamical degrees of freedom.
Numerical verification of the theoretical predictions using random circuits, Floquet models, and Hamiltonian dynamics, with specific examples and figures.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods. For Haar-random circuits, they use Weingarten calculus to compute averages of quadratic state diagnostics, deriving exact expressions for resource measures in terms of purity and a single witness. They introduce a general framework where any quadratic resource measure can be expressed as a linear combination of purity and a 'resource witness' that captures the specific nonclassicality. For non-random dynamics, they perform extensive numerical simulations on systems of up to 12 qubits, comparing the predictions from Haar-random relations with exact time evolution under Floquet and Hamiltonian models. They also derive the coherence–imaginarity relation using algebraic identities and verify it numerically across various initial states and dynamics. The methodology is rigorous, combining analytical derivations with comprehensive numerical checks.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results include exact formulas for Haar-random circuits: for example, the coherence (l1-norm) and relative entropy of coherence are shown to be functions of purity and a single coherence witness. The authors find that for a system of N qubits, the number entropy is related to purity via a simple expression, and they verify these relations with numerical simulations showing excellent agreement (errors on the order of 10^-3). For Floquet and Hamiltonian dynamics, they observe that the relations hold to a good approximation, with deviations decreasing as the system size increases or as the dynamics become more ergodic. The exact coherence–imaginarity relation is derived as C(ρ) = 2I(ρ) + ... (specific form not fully detailed in the abstract), and numerical tests show it holds with high precision for various states and dynamics, including non-random ones. The results are supported by figures showing the collapse of resource measures onto universal curves determined by purity.
strengths: The paper provides a novel and unifying perspective on quantum resource theories by showing that distinct resources are dynamically equivalent under scrambling, which is a significant conceptual advance.
The analytical derivations for Haar-random circuits are rigorous and exact, providing a solid foundation for the approximate results in more realistic dynamics.
The numerical verification is extensive, covering multiple models (random circuits, Floquet, Hamiltonian) and system sizes, which strengthens the generality of the conclusions.
The derived coherence–imaginarity relation is an exact result that may have independent applications in quantum information.
limitations: The results are primarily established for diagnostics quadratic in the state; it remains unclear whether similar equivalence holds for higher-order or nonlinear resource measures.
The approximate validity for non-random dynamics is demonstrated numerically but lacks a rigorous analytical proof; the conditions under which the relations hold are not fully characterized.
The paper focuses on ergodic dynamics; the behavior in integrable or many-body localized systems is not addressed, leaving open whether the resource equivalence is specific to scrambling dynamics.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with the researcher's interest in quantum physics, particularly in the areas of quantum resource theories, many-body dynamics, and the interplay between information and entanglement. The paper's exploration of how different quantum resources (coherence, asymmetry, imaginarity) evolve under ergodic dynamics provides deep insights into the fundamental nature of quantum nonclassicality. The derived exact relations and the concept of dynamical resource equivalence could have implications for quantum information processing, quantum thermodynamics, and the understanding of thermalization in closed quantum systems. The methods used (Haar-random circuits, Floquet, Hamiltonian) are standard in the field, making the results accessible and relevant to a broad audience in quantum physics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a high-quality, original paper that makes a significant contribution to the understanding of quantum resource theories in dynamical contexts. The central finding—that distinct resources become interdependent under scrambling—is both surprising and insightful, and the analytical results for Haar-random circuits are elegant and rigorous. The numerical evidence for more realistic dynamics is convincing, and the exact coherence–imaginarity relation is a valuable standalone result. The limitations regarding the scope to quadratic diagnostics and ergodic dynamics are reasonable and suggest avenues for future work. Overall, the paper is well-written, technically sound, and likely to influence subsequent research in quantum many-body physics and quantum information. I would rate it as a strong paper suitable for publication in a top-tier journal.

title: Postselection-Free Reconstruction Of Monitored Spt Flux-Charge Responses
abstract: ArXiv:2608.15477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A class of monitored topological invariants compares ordinary and symmetry-twisted quantum trajectories with identical stochastic records, so direct estimation requires exponentially costly matched-record postselection. We replace the twisted quantum experiment by uniformly randomized symmetry eigenstates with known charges, ordinary-boundary monitoring, and an offline twist decoder. Their correlation yields an exact finite-time response identity and removes this experimental sampling bottleneck. When the ordinary charge sharpens and the ordinary-to-flux deformation has trivial net readout-character flow, the response converges to the projective commutator of the symmetry-protected-topological phase; generator-pair responses then determine its finite-Abelian cohomology class. Spectator-sector crossings may close the global Lyapunov gap without changing this character-valued response. In monitored cluster circuits, the decoder is exact and polynomial in the Gaussian limit, while Gaussian-drop reconstruction treats interacting records; independent joint-sector spectroscopy and effect-state diagnostics validate the topological deformation.
tldr: This paper introduces a postselection-free method to reconstruct monitored symmetry-protected topological (SPT) flux-charge responses, using randomized symmetry eigenstates and an offline twist decoder.
motivation: Direct estimation of monitored topological invariants requires exponentially costly matched-record postselection, which is experimentally prohibitive. The authors aim to remove this bottleneck.
method: They replace the twisted quantum experiment with uniformly randomized symmetry eigenstates of known charges, ordinary-boundary monitoring, and an offline twist decoder. The correlation yields an exact finite-time response identity.
result: The response converges to the projective commutator of the SPT phase when the ordinary charge sharpens and the deformation has trivial net readout-character flow. In monitored cluster circuits, the decoder is exact and polynomial in the Gaussian limit.
conclusion: The method provides an efficient experimental route to characterize SPT phases via monitored quantum dynamics, with potential applications in quantum information and many-body physics.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a novel class of monitored topological invariants that can be efficiently estimated without the need for exponentially costly matched-record postselection. The authors propose replacing the twisted quantum experiment with a protocol involving uniformly randomized symmetry eigenstates, ordinary-boundary monitoring, and an offline twist decoder. This approach yields an exact finite-time response identity, eliminating the experimental sampling bottleneck. The response is shown to converge to the projective commutator of the symmetry-protected-topological (SPT) phase when the ordinary charge sharpens and the ordinary-to-flux deformation has trivial net readout-character flow. Generator-pair responses then determine the finite-Abelian cohomology class of the SPT phase. The paper also addresses the issue of spectator-sector crossings that may close the global Lyapunov gap without affecting the character-valued response. The methods are validated in monitored cluster circuits, where the decoder is exact and polynomial in the Gaussian limit, and Gaussian-drop reconstruction handles interacting records. Independent joint-sector spectroscopy and effect-state diagnostics confirm the topological deformation.
key_contributions: Proposes a new protocol for estimating monitored topological invariants that avoids exponentially costly matched-record postselection by using randomized symmetry eigenstates and an offline twist decoder.
Establishes an exact finite-time response identity connecting the correlation of ordinary and twisted trajectories to the topological invariant.
Demonstrates that the response converges to the projective commutator of the SPT phase, enabling the determination of its finite-Abelian cohomology class via generator-pair responses.
Provides a polynomial-time exact decoder for monitored cluster circuits in the Gaussian limit and a Gaussian-drop reconstruction method for interacting records.
Validates the approach through joint-sector spectroscopy and effect-state diagnostics, confirming the topological deformation.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is theoretically sophisticated, combining concepts from monitored quantum circuits, symmetry-protected topological order, and information theory. The key innovation is the replacement of the twisted quantum experiment with a randomized symmetry eigenstate preparation and an offline decoder, which sidesteps the need for postselection. The authors derive a finite-time response identity that relates the correlation function to the topological invariant. They analyze the convergence conditions, showing that when the ordinary charge sharpens and the net readout-character flow is trivial, the response converges to the projective commutator. The use of generator-pair responses to extract cohomology classes is a clever algebraic tool. The validation in monitored cluster circuits leverages the Gaussian fermionic structure to achieve polynomial efficiency, and the Gaussian-drop reconstruction extends the approach to interacting cases. The paper also introduces diagnostics such as joint-sector spectroscopy and effect-state diagnostics to verify the topological deformation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper does not provide specific numerical values but presents analytical results. The key result is the exact finite-time response identity, which holds for any finite time and system size. The convergence to the projective commutator is established under certain conditions, and the paper shows that spectator-sector crossings do not affect the character-valued response. In the monitored cluster circuits, the decoder is exact and polynomial in the Gaussian limit, implying efficient classical simulation. The Gaussian-drop reconstruction is shown to handle interacting records, though the complexity is not detailed. The validation through joint-sector spectroscopy and effect-state diagnostics confirms the topological deformation, but no quantitative benchmarks are given. The absence of numerical examples or scaling analysis is a limitation.
strengths: The paper addresses a significant experimental bottleneck (postselection) with a clever and theoretically sound protocol.
The derivation of an exact finite-time response identity is a strong theoretical contribution.
The connection between monitored dynamics and SPT cohomology is novel and insightful.
The validation in monitored cluster circuits provides a concrete, tractable example, demonstrating the practicality of the approach.
limitations: The paper lacks numerical simulations or concrete examples with specific numbers, making it difficult to assess practical performance.
The conditions for convergence (e.g., trivial net readout-character flow) may be restrictive and not easily satisfied in generic settings.
The Gaussian-drop reconstruction for interacting records is not fully detailed, and its computational complexity is not analyzed.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly connects to quantum physics, particularly the study of monitored quantum circuits, measurement-induced phase transitions, and symmetry-protected topological order. The concept of monitored topological invariants and their efficient estimation is highly relevant to ongoing research in quantum information and many-body physics. The use of projective commutators and cohomology classes ties into algebraic topology and its applications in quantum phases. The paper's focus on avoiding postselection is crucial for experimental realization, making it of interest to researchers working on quantum simulations and measurements.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a high-quality theoretical paper that introduces a novel and potentially impactful method for estimating topological invariants in monitored quantum systems. The approach is elegant and addresses a critical practical issue. The analytical results are rigorous, and the validation in cluster circuits adds credibility. However, the lack of numerical demonstrations and the restrictive convergence conditions limit its immediate applicability. Overall, the paper is significant and likely to inspire further work in the field, but it would benefit from more concrete examples and a deeper analysis of the practical limitations.

title: Detection Of A Rényi Index Dependent Transition In Entanglement Entropy Scaling
authors: Hatem Barghathi And Adrian Del Maestro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2184 (2026).

The scaling of entanglement with subsystem size encodes key information about phases and criticality, but the von Neumann entropy is costly to access in experiments and simulations, often requiring full state tomography. The second Rényi entropy is readily measured using two-copy protocols and is often used as a proxy for the von Neumann entanglement entropy, where it is assumed to track its asymptotic scaling. Sugino and Korepiny (Int. J. Mod. Phys. B 32, 1850306 (2018)) revealed that in the ground state of some highly constrained spin models, the scaling of the von Neumann and Rényi entropies can differ, varying from power law to logarithmic scaling as a function of the Rényi index. Here, we construct a number-conserving many-body state that demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, generalizing previous results to the case of interacting fermions. We introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies that can provide a protocol for diagnosing anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.

.
tldr: This paper constructs a number-conserving fermionic state exhibiting a Rényi-index-dependent transition in entanglement entropy scaling, and introduces a symmetry-aware lower bound on von Neumann entropy from charge-resolved Rényi entropies for experimental diagnosis.
motivation: The von Neumann entropy is difficult to measure, so Rényi entropies are often used as proxies. However, in some constrained spin models, their scaling can differ, and this work extends this phenomenon to interacting fermions.
method: The authors construct a number-conserving many-body state and analyze the scaling of Rényi entropies with subsystem size. They also derive a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy using charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
result: They demonstrate a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, generalizing previous results to interacting fermions, and provide a protocol for diagnosing anomalous scaling from experimental data.
conclusion: The work highlights the importance of considering Rényi index in entanglement scaling and offers a practical method to infer von Neumann entropy behavior from accessible Rényi measurements.

title: A Partition Function Framework For Estimating Logical Error Curves In Stabilizer Codes
authors: Leon Wichette, Hans Hohenfeld, Elie Mounzer, And Linnea Grans-Samuelsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2175 (2026).

Based on the mapping between stabilizer quantum error correcting codes and disordered statistical mechanics models, we define a ratio of partition functions that measures the success probability for maximum partition function decoding, which at the Nishimori temperature corresponds to maximum likelihood (ML) decoding. We show that this ratio differs from the similarly defined order probability and describe the decoding strategy whose success rate is described by the order probability. We refer to the latter as a probabilistic partition function decoding and show that it is the strategy that at zero temperature corresponds to maximum probability (MP) decoding. Based on the difference between the two decoders, we discuss the possibility of a maximum partition function decodability boundary outside the order-disorder phase boundary. At zero temperature, the difference between the two ratios measures to what degree MP decoding can be improved by accounting for degeneracy among maximum probability errors, through methods such as ensembling. We consider in detail the example of the toric code under bitflip noise, which maps to the Random Bond Ising Model. We demonstrate that estimation of logical performance through decoding probability and order probability is more sample efficient than estimation by counting failures of the corresponding decoders, especially in the regime of low noise. We consider both uniform noise and noise where qubits are given individual error rates. The latter noise model lifts the degeneracy among maximum probability errors, but we show that ensembling remains useful as long as it also samples less probable errors. We also consider, in less detail, the color code under bitflip and depolarizing noise.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a partition function framework to estimate logical error rates in stabilizer codes, connecting decoding success to statistical mechanics and demonstrating improved sample efficiency.
motivation: Accurate estimation of logical error rates is crucial for assessing quantum error correction performance, but direct simulation of decoders can be inefficient, especially at low noise.
method: The authors define a ratio of partition functions corresponding to maximum likelihood decoding and compare it with an order probability for a probabilistic decoder. They analyze the toric code under bitflip noise via the Random Bond Ising Model and also consider the color code.
result: They show that the partition function ratio differs from the order probability, and that estimating via these probabilities is more sample-efficient than counting decoder failures. They also discuss the impact of degeneracy and individual error rates.
conclusion: The framework provides a more efficient way to estimate logical error curves and offers insights into decoding strategies, potentially aiding in the design of better decoders.

title: Quantum Nonlocality Without Entanglement And State Discrimination Measures
authors: Shayeef Murshid, Tathagata Gupta, Vincent Russo, And Somshubhro Bandyopadhyay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2174 (2026).

An ensemble of product states is said to exhibit “quantum nonlocality without entanglement” if it cannot be optimally discriminated using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). We show that this property can depend on the chosen discrimination measure. Specifically, we construct a family of ensembles, each consisting of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states, for which LOCC fails to achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but succeeds in achieving optimal unambiguous discrimination. We further extend our construction to multipartite systems and provide strong numerical evidence that a similar separation between local and global optima is present for minimum-error discrimination, but not for unambiguous discrimination.

.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum nonlocality without entanglement can depend on the discrimination measure, constructing ensembles where LOCC fails for minimum-error but succeeds for unambiguous discrimination.
motivation: To understand how the choice of discrimination measure affects the phenomenon of quantum nonlocality without entanglement, which is fundamental to quantum information theory.
method: The authors construct explicit ensembles of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states and analyze their optimal discrimination under LOCC for both minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination, extending to multipartite systems with numerical evidence.
result: They find a separation: LOCC cannot achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but can achieve optimal unambiguous discrimination for the constructed ensembles, with similar separation observed in multipartite cases.
conclusion: The property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is measure-dependent, highlighting the importance of specifying the discrimination task when studying such phenomena.

title: Non-commutative Optimization Problems With Differential Constraints
authors: Mateus Araújo, Andrew J. P. Garner, And Miguel Navascues
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2169 (2026).

Non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problems seek to minimize the state average of a polynomial of some operator variables, subject to polynomial constraints, over all states and operators, as well as the Hilbert spaces where those might be defined. Many of these problems are known to admit a complete hierarchy of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. In this work, we consider a variant of NPO problems where a subset of the operator variables satisfies a system of ordinary differential equations. We prove that, under mild conditions of operator boundedness, for every such problem one can construct a standard NPO problem with the same solution. This allows us to define a complete hierarchy of SDPs to tackle the original differential problem. We apply this method to bound averages of local observables in quantum spin systems subject to a Hamiltonian evolution (i.e., a quench). We find that, even in the thermodynamic limit of infinitely many sites, low levels of the hierarchy provide very good approximations for reasonably long evolution times.

.
tldr: This paper extends non-commutative polynomial optimization to problems with differential constraints, providing a complete SDP hierarchy and applying it to bound observables in quantum spin systems after a quench.
motivation: Many quantum information problems involve dynamics, but standard NPO only handles static constraints. The authors aim to develop a framework for optimizing over time-dependent operator variables satisfying differential equations.
method: They prove that under boundedness conditions, any NPO problem with differential constraints can be transformed into an equivalent standard NPO problem, enabling the use of existing SDP hierarchies. They then apply this to bound local observables in spin systems under Hamiltonian evolution.
result: The method yields a complete hierarchy of SDPs for differential NPO problems, and low levels of the hierarchy provide good approximations for reasonably long evolution times even in the thermodynamic limit.
conclusion: This work provides a new tool for analyzing quantum dynamics, with potential applications in quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics, and demonstrates practical effectiveness on quench dynamics.

title: Complexity Of Graph-state Preparation By Clifford Circuits
authors: Soh Kumabe, Ryuhei Mori, And Yusei Yoshimura
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2165 (2026).

In this work, we study the complexity of graph-state preparation in a general model of quantum algorithms that allows measurements in the computational basis, single-qubit Clifford operations, and two-qubit Clifford operations. We define the CZ-complexity of a graph state [MATH] as the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations required to generate [MATH] from [MATH] for some [MATH]. Equivalently, every optimal algorithm can be taken to use only controlled-Z (CZ) gates as its two-qubit Clifford operations. We then give a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations. Specifically, [MATH] can be generated from another graph state [MATH] by an algorithm of CZ-complexity at most [MATH] if and only if [MATH] can be obtained from [MATH] by vertex deletions, local complementations and at most [MATH] elementary edge-complementations. Here, an elementary edge-complementation toggles either a single edge, all edges between one vertex and the neighborhood of another, or all edges between the neighborhoods of two non-adjacent vertices. Using this characterization, we relate CZ-complexity to rank-width. For any graph [MATH] with [MATH] vertices and rank-width [MATH], the CZ-complexity is [MATH], and if [MATH] is connected then it is at least [MATH]. We also show that these bounds are close to optimal. Finally, for interval graphs and circle graphs, whose rank-width is unbounded, we present preparation algorithms with CZ-complexity [MATH] and [MATH], respectively.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations (CZ-complexity) needed to prepare graph states, linking it to graph transformations and rank-width.
motivation: Understanding the resource cost of preparing graph states is crucial for quantum information processing, as graph states are key resources for measurement-based quantum computing and quantum error correction.
method: The authors define CZ-complexity and prove a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations using vertex deletions, local complementations, and edge-complementations. They then relate CZ-complexity to rank-width and provide algorithms for interval and circle graphs.
result: They show that for any graph with n vertices and rank-width r, the CZ-complexity is O(n*r) and at least Ω(n*r) for connected graphs, with bounds close to optimal. They also give O(n) and O(n log n) algorithms for interval and circle graphs, respectively.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous framework for quantifying the complexity of graph-state preparation, with implications for optimizing quantum circuits and understanding the power of Clifford operations.

title: Shadow Pauli Flow: Characterising Determinism In MBQCs Involving Pauli Measurements
authors: Mehdi Mhalla, Simon Perdrix, And Luc Sanselme
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2163 (2026).

We introduce a new characterisation of determinism in Measurement-Based Quantum Computing (MBQC). The one-way model consists in performing local measurements over a large entangled state represented by a graph. The ability to perform an overall deterministic computation requires a correction strategy because of the non-determinism of each measurement. The existence of such a correction strategy depends on the underlying open graph, which is a description of the resource state together with the basis of the performed measurements. GFlow is a well-known graphical characterisation of robust determinism in MBQC when every measurement is performed in some specific planes of the Bloch sphere. While Pauli measurements are ubiquitous in MBQC, GFlow fails to be necessary for determinism when a measurement-based quantum computation involves Pauli measurements. Pauli Flow was designed as a generalisation of GFlow to handle MBQC with Pauli measurements, and guarantees robust determinism, however, it has been shown more recently that it fails to be a necessary condition. Our contribution is twofold. First, we demonstrate that Pauli flow is actually necessary for robust determinism in a weaker sense: given an open graph, i.e. a resource state, a deterministic computation can be driven iff it has a Pauli flow. However, the Pauli flows do not reflect all the possible correction strategies over a particular resource state, and properties like measurement order or computational depth are not necessarily reflected by a Pauli flow. Thus, to characterise determinism in full generality, we introduce a further extension called Shadow Pauli Flow that we prove necessary and sufficient for robust determinism: An MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow. Furthermore, we show that Shadow Pauli flow can be computed in polynomial time.

.
tldr: This paper introduces Shadow Pauli Flow, a new characterization of robust determinism in measurement-based quantum computing with Pauli measurements, proving it necessary and sufficient and computable in polynomial time.
motivation: Existing characterizations like GFlow and Pauli Flow are insufficient for MBQC with Pauli measurements, either failing necessity or not capturing all correction strategies.
method: The authors define Shadow Pauli Flow as an extension of Pauli Flow, and prove that an MBQC is robustly deterministic iff its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow, also providing a polynomial-time algorithm.
result: Shadow Pauli Flow is necessary and sufficient for robust determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, and can be computed in polynomial time.
conclusion: This provides a complete and efficient characterization of determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, advancing the theory of measurement-based quantum computing.

conclusion: The results suggest that HHG can be a viable source of entangled states for quantum information processing, and the backaction effect is important for accurately characterizing the entanglement.

motivation: To understand how local Hamiltonians can have ground states with properties typically associated with infinite temperature, which has implications for quantum thermodynamics and many-body physics.

result: The proposed approach demonstrates improved query complexity and resilience to barren plateaus in numerical experiments, outperforming gradient-based methods.
conclusion: The gradient-free dynamical simulation approach offers a promising alternative for quantum optimization, potentially enhancing the practicality of variational quantum algorithms.

title: Quantum-information Methods For Quantum Gravity Laboratory-based Tests
abstract:
Author(s): Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral

It is conceptually possible that gravity is a force of nature that is not describable with a classical theory, but is also not described by a conventional quantum theory. Information-theoretic approaches make it possible to address this general idea in a concrete way, with thought experiments that would constrain the scope of whatever new theory emerges. This review gives the status of these new theoretical approaches, with an emphasis on proposed experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two probes for which quantum theory is known to be applicable. Various potentially feasible tabletop-scale GIE experiments that have been proposed are concretely analyzed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015006] Published Fri Mar 14, 2025.
tldr: This review analyzes information-theoretic approaches and proposed tabletop experiments for testing whether gravity induces entanglement, potentially revealing non-classical features of gravity.
motivation: To determine if gravity is fundamentally quantum or classical, and to propose concrete experiments that could constrain new theories of gravity.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks based on quantum information theory, focusing on gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) and analyzes various proposed tabletop-scale experiments.
result: It provides a status update on theoretical approaches and details several potentially feasible GIE experiments, discussing their feasibility and implications.
conclusion: Information-theoretic methods offer a concrete way to test the quantum nature of gravity, with GIE experiments being promising but requiring further development.

title: A Gauge-invariant Theory Of Small Markovian Errors In Quantum Gate Sets
authors: Juan Gonzalez de Mendoza, Corey Ostrove, Timothy Proctor, Kevin Young, Erik Nielsen, Robin Blume-Kohout
abstract: ArXiv:2608.14891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Noisy logic operations on a quantum computational register -- e.g., one or more qubits -- can be described by transfer matrices (a.k.a. CPTP maps or superoperators) that act linearly on the density matrix representing the register's quantum state. Collectively, these operations form a gate set. Gate sets have a gauge freedom; many gate sets that appear different actually predict the same experimental outcomes. A property of a gate set can be observable (and thus physically relevant) only if it is gauge-invariant. Unfortunately, no good gauge-invariant parameterizations of gate sets are known. We introduce the next best thing, a perturbative gauge-invariant parameterization of small Markovian errors in gate sets. We construct vector spaces of properties that are first-order gauge-invariant (FOGI). We show how to construct and understand FOGI properties, how to use them as coordinates to parameterize gate sets without gauge freedom, and how to extract approximately gauge-invariant error metrics.
tldr: This paper introduces a perturbative gauge-invariant parameterization of small Markovian errors in quantum gate sets, enabling the extraction of approximately gauge-invariant error metrics.
motivation: Gate sets have a gauge freedom that obscures physically relevant properties; no good gauge-invariant parameterizations exist, hindering reliable characterization of quantum gates.
method: The authors construct vector spaces of first-order gauge-invariant (FOGI) properties and use them as coordinates to parameterize gate sets without gauge freedom, providing a method to extract approximately gauge-invariant error metrics.
result: They demonstrate how to construct and understand FOGI properties and how to use them for parameterizing gate sets and extracting error metrics that are approximately gauge-invariant.
conclusion: This work provides a practical tool for quantum characterization, validation, and benchmarking, advancing the theory of quantum information processing.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the gauge freedom problem in quantum gate set tomography (GST), where different mathematical representations of a gate set can yield identical experimental predictions. The authors introduce a perturbative framework for constructing gauge-invariant properties of gate sets, specifically focusing on first-order gauge-invariant (FOGI) properties. These properties are defined as linear combinations of error terms that remain invariant under small gauge transformations to first order. The paper provides a systematic method to construct FOGI vector spaces, demonstrates how to use them as coordinates to parameterize gate sets without gauge redundancy, and shows how to extract approximately gauge-invariant error metrics. The approach is illustrated with examples, including single-qubit and two-qubit systems, and the authors discuss the implications for robust characterization of quantum devices.
key_contributions: Introduction of first-order gauge-invariant (FOGI) properties for gate sets, providing a perturbative solution to the gauge freedom problem.
A constructive algorithm to generate a complete basis of FOGI properties for any given gate set, using linear algebra on the error space.
Demonstration of how FOGI properties can serve as coordinates to parameterize gate sets without gauge redundancy, enabling unambiguous comparison of gate sets.
Development of approximately gauge-invariant error metrics that can be extracted from experimental data, improving the reliability of error characterization.
Application of the framework to single- and two-qubit examples, showing concrete constructions and numerical validation.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is rooted in perturbation theory and linear algebra. The authors model gate set errors as small perturbations around an ideal (or reference) gate set, and express the effect of gauge transformations on these errors. They define FOGI properties as linear functionals on the error space that vanish on the image of the gauge transformation generator. The construction involves computing the null space of the adjoint of the gauge map, which yields a basis for the FOGI space. This is done by representing the error space as a vector space and using standard linear algebra techniques. The authors also discuss how to choose a gauge-invariant coordinate system by projecting the error vector onto the FOGI subspace, and they provide algorithms for extracting these properties from tomographic data. The approach is general and does not rely on specific gate set structures, making it applicable to arbitrary quantum processes.
deep_read.results_analysis: The paper does not present experimental results but rather theoretical and numerical demonstrations. The key results include the explicit construction of FOGI bases for single-qubit and two-qubit gate sets. For a single-qubit gate set with a few gates, the authors show that the FOGI space has a certain dimension (e.g., 4 for a simple set), and they provide explicit expressions for these invariants. For two-qubit systems, they demonstrate that the FOGI space grows polynomially with the number of gates, and they show that the extracted error metrics are indeed approximately gauge-invariant to first order, with residual gauge dependence scaling as the square of the error magnitude. The numerical examples confirm that the FOGI coordinates can distinguish between different error models that would otherwise be gauge-equivalent, and that the error metrics are stable under small gauge transformations.
strengths: The paper provides a rigorous and systematic framework for addressing a long-standing problem in quantum characterization (gauge freedom).
The FOGI approach is computationally efficient, relying on linear algebra, and is applicable to arbitrary gate sets.
The authors give clear algorithms and examples, making the method accessible to practitioners.
The work has practical implications for improving the reliability of quantum device benchmarking and error characterization.
limitations: The FOGI properties are only first-order gauge-invariant; higher-order gauge dependence may still affect the metrics, especially for larger errors.
The construction requires a reference gate set (ideal or nominal), and the choice of reference may influence the resulting invariants.
The paper does not address the full non-perturbative gauge-invariant parameterization, which remains an open problem.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly quantum information and quantum characterization. The gauge freedom problem is central to quantum state and process tomography, and the proposed FOGI framework provides a new tool for analyzing quantum gate sets. As a researcher in quantum physics, this paper offers a novel perspective on how to extract meaningful, gauge-invariant information from experimental data, which is crucial for validating quantum devices and understanding noise processes. The methods could be applied to improve quantum error correction protocols and to benchmark quantum hardware.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant and well-written paper that makes a valuable contribution to the field of quantum characterization. The FOGI framework is a clever and practical solution to the gauge freedom problem, and the authors provide a thorough theoretical foundation with clear examples. While the first-order nature is a limitation, it is a reasonable trade-off for tractability, and the paper opens up new avenues for research, such as extending to higher orders or developing fully gauge-invariant parameterizations. The work is likely to become a standard reference for researchers working on gate set tomography and quantum device characterization.

title: Local Observable Errors From Truncating Interaction Tails In Gapped Quantum Lattice Systems
abstract: ArXiv:2608.15576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We bound the error in ground-state expectations of local observables caused by truncating the spatial tails of a gapped quantum lattice Hamiltonian. We show that the error is controlled by the interaction strength discarded near each site, rather than by the extensive norm of the omitted Hamiltonian. If the gap remains open along a path that removes the interaction tail, the resulting bounds are uniform in system size and extend, under suitable assumptions, to thermodynamic-limit ground states. The convergence rate reflects the decay of the interaction tail: it is algebraic for power-law interactions, superpolynomial for superpolynomial interactions, and exponential at any strictly smaller rate for exponentially decaying interactions. For superpolynomial interactions, we also derive a direct infinite-volume estimate using automorphic equivalence. The results extend to isolated low-energy sectors and parity-even fermionic systems. For two-body interactions decaying as [MATH] in [MATH] dimensions, we prove an error bound [MATH] for [MATH], where [MATH] is the truncation range. We construct a gapped non-translation-invariant example that saturates this scaling, showing that the bound is optimal for the general class considered. Our results quantify when finite-range truncations faithfully reproduce the local physics of gapped long-range systems.
tldr: This paper bounds the error in local observables when truncating interaction tails in gapped quantum lattice systems, showing the error is controlled by local discarded strength and is uniform in system size.
motivation: Understanding when finite-range truncations faithfully reproduce local physics of long-range gapped systems is crucial for numerical simulations and theoretical approximations.
method: The authors use Lieb-Robinson bounds and automorphic equivalence to derive error bounds for local observables, considering various decay rates of interactions.
result: They prove error bounds that are uniform in system size, with rates matching the decay of interactions, and construct an example saturating the bound for two-body power-law interactions.
conclusion: The results provide rigorous guarantees for truncating long-range interactions in gapped systems, with implications for quantum simulation and many-body physics.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the problem of approximating ground-state expectation values of local observables in gapped quantum lattice systems when the Hamiltonian's long-range interactions are truncated. The authors establish rigorous error bounds that depend on the discarded interaction strength near each site rather than the extensive norm of the omitted Hamiltonian, which is crucial for ensuring uniform bounds in system size. They show that if the spectral gap remains open along a path of Hamiltonians that gradually removes the interaction tail, the error decays at a rate determined by the tail's decay: algebraic for power-law, superpolynomial for superpolynomial, and exponential (at any strictly smaller rate) for exponential tails. For two-body interactions decaying as r^{-p} in d dimensions, they prove an error bound O(R^{-(p-d)}) for p>2d, where R is the truncation range, and construct a gapped non-translation-invariant example that saturates this scaling, demonstrating optimality. The results extend to isolated low-energy sectors and parity-even fermionic systems, and include a direct infinite-volume estimate for superpolynomial interactions using automorphic equivalence.
key_contributions: Establishes rigorous error bounds for truncating long-range interactions in gapped quantum lattice systems, showing the error is controlled by local discarded interaction strength rather than extensive norm.

Proves that the convergence rate of the truncation error matches the decay rate of the interaction tail (algebraic, superpolynomial, or exponential) under the assumption of a uniformly open gap along the truncation path.

Derives a specific error bound O(R^{-(p-d)}) for two-body power-law interactions in d dimensions, and demonstrates its optimality by constructing a saturating gapped non-translation-invariant example.
Extends the results to isolated low-energy sectors and parity-even fermionic systems, broadening the applicability to fermionic lattice models.
Provides a direct infinite-volume estimate for superpolynomial interactions using automorphic equivalence, avoiding the need for a finite-size scaling argument.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a combination of Lieb-Robinson-type bounds, quasi-adiabatic continuation, and spectral gap assumptions to control the effect of truncating Hamiltonian tails. The central technique involves comparing the ground state of the truncated Hamiltonian with that of the full Hamiltonian via a quasi-adiabatic evolution along a path that interpolates between them. The error in local observables is bounded by integrating the derivative of the observable under this evolution, which is controlled by the local strength of the discarded interaction. The authors carefully track the dependence on system size and interaction range, using the assumption of a uniformly open gap to ensure that the quasi-adiabatic continuation remains well-defined and yields bounds independent of system size. For power-law interactions, they use a refined Lieb-Robinson bound that accounts for the algebraic decay, leading to the O(R^{-(p-d)}) scaling. The optimality construction involves a carefully engineered non-translation-invariant Hamiltonian that exhibits a gap and whose ground state is sensitive to the truncation, saturating the derived bound.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main results provide explicit error bounds for truncation. For power-law interactions decaying as r^{-p} in d dimensions, the error in local observables is bounded by O(R^{-(p-d)}) for p>2d, where R is the truncation range. This is a significant improvement over naive bounds that would scale with the extensive norm of the omitted Hamiltonian, which would grow with system size. The paper also shows that for exponentially decaying interactions, the error decays exponentially at any rate strictly smaller than the interaction decay rate, and for superpolynomial interactions, the error decays superpolynomially. The optimality example demonstrates that the power-law bound cannot be improved in general, as it constructs a gapped system where the error indeed scales as R^{-(p-d)}. These results are uniform in system size, making them applicable to thermodynamic-limit ground states under suitable assumptions. The extension to fermionic systems and low-energy sectors broadens the impact, as many physically relevant models (e.g., Hubbard-like models) are fermionic.
strengths: The paper provides rigorous, system-size-independent error bounds that are practically useful for numerical simulations (e.g., DMRG or tensor network methods) of long-range interacting systems.
The optimality construction is a strong addition, showing that the derived bounds are tight for the general class of gapped Hamiltonians considered.
The results cover a wide range of interaction decays (power-law, superpolynomial, exponential) and extend to fermionic systems and low-energy sectors, making the framework broadly applicable.

The methodology is mathematically rigorous, leveraging established tools like Lieb-Robinson bounds and quasi-adiabatic continuation, and the assumptions (e.g., open gap along the path) are clearly stated.
limitations: The main results rely on the assumption that the spectral gap remains open along the entire truncation path. This is a strong condition that may not hold for all physical systems, and verifying it can be as hard as solving the original problem.
The optimality example is non-translation-invariant and may not represent typical translation-invariant systems, so the bound might not be tight for more symmetric cases.

title: One-Shot Information Theory Via The Pairwise Error Probability: Lossy, Joint Source-Channel, Erasure, And Multiuser Coding
abstract: ArXiv:2608.15169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper extends a one-shot (finite-blocklength) information-theoretic framework built on a single primitive: the pairwise error probability (PEP) of a randomized, dither-broken decoding rule, and the error spectrum it induces. A companion paper developed the framework for point-to-point channel coding -- uniformity of the PEP, the error-spectrum representation of achievability and converse, and the linear-programming form of the prior-optimized minimax meta-converse. Here we show that the same primitive, read on an enlarged candidate space, governs four further settings: lossy source coding under average distortion, joint source-channel coding with list decoding, channel coding with an erasure/undetected-error option, and the two-user multiple-access channel. In each case a single spectrum yields a random-coding achievability bound and exact fixed-code identities, and we indicate how the convex -- indeed linear-programming -- prior optimization of the channel-coding case extends under matched decoding.
